title: Unification of Upper and Lower Egypt
summary: Tradition credits Narmer with joining the two lands and founding the First Dynasty.
body: Later king lists and the Narmer Palette are the usual evidence; unification was likely a longer process than a single campaign. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Wilkinson, Early Dynastic Egypt

title: Great Pyramid of Giza
summary: Khufu’s pyramid becomes the defining monument of Old Kingdom royal power.
body: Built on the Giza plateau as a tomb and a statement of administrative capacity, it remained the tallest human-made structure for millennia. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Lehner, The Complete Pyramids

title: Sargon of Akkad
summary: Sargon forges one of the first large territorial empires in Mesopotamia.
body: Akkadian rule tied together city-states from the Gulf toward the Mediterranean and left a template for later Near Eastern kingship. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Van de Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East

title: Code of Hammurabi
summary: The Babylonian king issues a monumental law collection now famous from a diorite stele.
body: The prologue, casuistic rulings, and carved relief present justice as a royal duty. The text is a window on Old Babylonian society, not a modern statute book. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Roth, Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor

title: Thera eruption
summary: A massive eruption on Thera devastates the Aegean and disrupts Minoan networks.
body: Ash, tsunami, and the destruction of Akrotiri are archaeologically clear; the exact calendar year and the link to Egyptian chronology remain debated. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Friedrich, The Minoan Eruption of Santorini

title: Reign of Hatshepsut
summary: Hatshepsut rules as pharaoh and sponsors major building and a famous Punt expedition.
body: Her monuments at Deir el-Bahri and later erasures make her one of the best-documented women to hold full pharaonic titles. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Tyldesley, Hatchepsut

title: Battle of Kadesh
summary: Ramesses II fights the Hittites in a chariot battle later commemorated in temple reliefs.
body: The campaign produced one of the earliest surviving peace treaties. Both sides claimed advantage; the political settlement mattered more than the clash itself. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Kitchen, Pharaoh Triumphant

title: Late Bronze Age collapse
summary: Palace economies around the eastern Mediterranean unravel within a few generations.
body: Letters from Ugarit, burnt layers, and the end of several scripts mark a systemic crisis. Drought, migration, trade shocks, and war are all in the mix. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Cline, 1177 B.C.

title: Olmec San Lorenzo florescence
summary: San Lorenzo becomes a major Olmec centre with colossal heads and long-distance exchange.
body: The Gulf Coast centres are among the earliest complex societies in Mesoamerica and a reference point for later Maya and highland cultures. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Pool, Olmec Archaeology and Early Mesoamerica

title: Zhou conquest of Shang
summary: The Zhou overthrow Shang and later justify the change as a Mandate of Heaven.
body: The date is conventional; the political shift created a feudal order and a moral language of legitimate rule that Chinese historiography never dropped. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Li Feng, Early China

title: Traditional first Olympiad
summary: Later Greeks dated their era from games held at Olympia in this year.
body: The festival mixed athletics, religion, and interstate display. The 776 date is a later chronological device, not a modern sports founding myth alone. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Finley and Pleket, The Olympic Games

title: Traditional founding of Rome
summary: Roman tradition places Romulus’s founding of the city in this year.
body: Archaeology shows earlier settlement on the hills. The date mattered because Romans used it to count ab urbe condita and to narrate their origins. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita; Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome

title: Fall of Nineveh
summary: A Median–Babylonian coalition captures the Assyrian capital and ends the neo-Assyrian empire.
body: Assyria had dominated the Near East for generations. The sack of Nineveh redistributed power toward Babylon and the Medes. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Van de Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East

title: Destruction of Jerusalem and exile
summary: Nebuchadnezzar II destroys the Temple and deports Judean elites to Babylon.
body: The exile reshaped Hebrew religion and literature. Return under the Persians is the other half of the story, not a simple restoration of the old kingdom. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: 2 Kings; Finkelstein and Silberman, The Bible Unearthed

title: Cyrus takes Babylon
summary: Cyrus the Great captures Babylon and folds it into the Achaemenid Empire.
body: The Cyrus Cylinder presents the king as a restorer of cults. Persian rule created a vast imperial system from the Aegean to the Indus. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander

title: Death of Confucius
summary: Kongzi dies after a life of teaching that later becomes the core of the Confucian canon.
body: The Analects were compiled by followers. His stress on ritual, filiality, and ethical government shaped East Asian political culture for two millennia. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Nylan, The Five “Confucian” Classics

title: Death of the Buddha (traditional)
summary: Siddhartha Gautama’s death marks, in tradition, the start of the Buddhist saṅgha’s long expansion.
body: Dating is debated (often later in the 5th–4th centuries). The teaching of dukkha, anatta, and the path travelled with merchants and monks across Asia. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Gethin, The Foundations of Buddhism

title: Battle of Marathon
summary: Athenian and Plataean hoplites defeat a Persian landing force on the Marathon plain.
body: The victory became a founding memory of Athenian freedom. It did not end the Persian Wars; that waited on Salamis and Plataea. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Herodotus, Histories

title: Battle of Salamis
summary: Greek allied fleets defeat Xerxes’ navy in the straits of Salamis.
body: After Thermopylae and the fall of Athens, the naval victory forced the Persian king to withdraw much of his force and set up Plataea. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Herodotus, Histories; Green, The Greco-Persian Wars

title: Parthenon begun
summary: Athens begins the Parthenon on the Acropolis under Pericles’ building programme.
body: The temple advertised Athenian wealth after the Persian Wars and housed a colossal Athena. Its sculptures remain a central—and contested—classical corpus. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Neils, The Parthenon

title: Peloponnesian War
summary: Athens and Sparta fight a generation-long war that breaks the classical Greek balance.
body: Thucydides’ history made the conflict a school for later realists. Plague, Sicily, and oligarchic coups matter as much as set-piece battles. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War

title: Death of Socrates
summary: Athens executes Socrates, an event Plato turns into a founding scene of Western philosophy.
body: The charges were impiety and corrupting the young. The trial sits at the junction of democracy, war trauma, and a new style of moral inquiry. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Plato, Apology; Xenophon, Memorabilia

title: Alexander’s Asian campaign
summary: Alexander of Macedon overthrows the Achaemenids and carries armies to the Indus.
body: His death at Babylon fragmented the conquest into Hellenistic kingdoms. Greek language and cities spread across the Near East without erasing local cultures. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Arrian, Anabasis; Bosworth, Conquest and Empire

title: Chandragupta founds the Maurya Empire
summary: Chandragupta Maurya builds a North Indian empire in the wake of Alexander’s withdrawal.
body: Greek and Indian traditions both notice him. The Maurya state became the first pan-Indian imperial structure for which we have substantial evidence. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Thapar, Early India

title: Ashoka and the Kalinga war
summary: After a bloody conquest of Kalinga, Ashoka advertises dhamma on inscriptions across the subcontinent.
body: The edicts are primary evidence. They mix Buddhist ethics, imperial communication, and a claim to rule by righteousness rather than terror alone. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Thapar, Aśoka and the Decline of the Mauryas

title: First Punic War
summary: Rome and Carthage fight a long naval war for Sicily.
body: Rome learned to fight at sea the hard way. Victory made Sicily the first Roman province and set up later showdowns with Carthage. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Polybius, Histories

title: Qin unification of China
summary: Qin Shi Huang completes the conquest of the Warring States and declares an empire.
body: Standard script, roads, harsh law, and massive labour projects followed. The dynasty was short; the imperial template lasted. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Lewis, The Early Chinese Empires

title: Battle of Cannae
summary: Hannibal encircles and destroys a larger Roman army in Apulia.
body: Cannae became the textbook double envelopment. Rome refused to collapse, a political fact as important as the tactical masterpiece. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Polybius, Histories; Livy, Ab Urbe Condita

title: Destruction of Carthage
summary: Rome razes Carthage at the end of the Third Punic War; Corinth falls the same year.
body: The two sackings advertised a new Mediterranean hierarchy. Africa became a Roman province; Greece was brought to heel. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Appian, Punica; Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome

title: Maccabean Revolt
summary: Judeans revolt against Seleucid policy, a struggle later remembered at Hanukkah.
body: 1 and 2 Maccabees are partisan but indispensable. The revolt produced the Hasmonean state and a long argument about law, empire, and cult. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: 1 Maccabees; Schwartz, Imperialism and Jewish Society

title: Assassination of Julius Caesar
summary: Senators kill Caesar on the Ides of March, accelerating the Republic’s collapse.
body: The murder did not restore senatorial liberty. Civil war followed, and Octavian emerged as Augustus. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Plutarch, Caesar; Suetonius, Divine Julius

title: Battle of Actium
summary: Octavian defeats Antony and Cleopatra at sea and is left master of the Roman world.
body: Egypt was annexed. The victory was packaged as the rescue of Rome from an eastern queen; it was also the end of the last Hellenistic dynasty that mattered. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Plutarch, Antony; Syme, The Roman Revolution

title: Augustus and the Principate
summary: Octavian takes the name Augustus and builds a monarchy dressed as restored Republic.
body: Provinces, army, grain, and city were reorganized. The settlement of 27 BCE is a convenient marker for the Roman Empire in this timeline. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Res Gestae Divi Augusti; Syme, The Roman Revolution

title: Birth of Jesus (conventional)
summary: Jesus of Nazareth is born in the last years of Herod, according to the usual historical reconstruction.
body: The Gospels are theological narratives, not civil registers. The movement that followed became the largest religious structure in later European and world history. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Meier, A Marginal Jew; Fredriksen, From Jesus to Christ

title: Claudian invasion of Britain
summary: Claudius sends an army that begins the Roman conquest of Britain.
body: Conquest was incomplete and expensive. Roman Britain lasted until the early 5th century and left roads, towns, and a frontier on the Tyne–Solway line. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Tacitus, Agricola; Salway, A History of Roman Britain

title: Destruction of the Second Temple
summary: Titus’s forces destroy the Temple at the climax of the Jewish War.
body: The loss of the sacrificial centre pushed Judaism toward rabbinic forms. Rome advertised the victory on the Arch of Titus. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Josephus, Jewish War

title: Eruption of Vesuvius
summary: Vesuvius buries Pompeii and Herculaneum, preserving an ordinary Roman world under ash.
body: Pliny the Younger’s letters are eyewitness literature. Archaeology at the sites remains a principal source for Roman daily life. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Pliny the Younger, Letters; Beard, Pompeii

title: Death of Trajan / imperial high-water
summary: Trajan dies after taking the empire to its greatest territorial extent.
body: Hadrian succeeded and retrenched. The Dacian and Parthian wars show both the reach and the cost of Roman expansion. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Bennett, Trajan

title: Antonine Plague
summary: A pandemic, possibly smallpox, spreads through the Roman world under Marcus Aurelius.
body: Mortality estimates vary wildly. The shock sits among the stresses that made the later 2nd and 3rd centuries harder to govern. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Harper, The Fate of Rome

title: Crisis of the Third Century
summary: Assassination, civil war, inflation, and invasions nearly break the Roman imperial system.
body: The Gallic and Palmyrene breakaways show how regional power filled the vacuum. Diocletian’s later tetrarchy is a response, not a restoration of the old Principate. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Potter, The Roman Empire at Bay

title: Battle of the Milvian Bridge
summary: Constantine defeats Maxentius and soon favours Christianity in imperial policy.
body: The vision stories are later and partisan. The political fact is that a Roman emperor tied his victory to the Christian God and changed the empire’s religious trajectory. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Eusebius, Life of Constantine; Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius

title: Council of Nicaea
summary: Bishops meeting under Constantine produce the Nicene Creed in the Arian controversy.
body: Imperial church councils became a tool of both theology and politics. Nicaea did not end the argument; it defined the terms. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Ayres, Nicaea and its Legacy

title: Gupta age in northern India
summary: Gupta rulers preside over a classical period of Sanskrit literature, mathematics, and temple culture.
body: The “golden age” label is later and partial. The period still concentrates much of what later Indian courts treated as a classical inheritance. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Thapar, Early India

title: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
summary: Odoacer deposes the last western emperor, a conventional date for the “fall of Rome.”
body: The eastern empire continued from Constantinople. In the west, barbarian kingdoms ruled a still-Roman landscape. 476 is a bookmark, not an extinction. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire; Ward-Perkins, The Fall of Rome

title: Justinian’s Corpus Juris Civilis
summary: Justinian’s commissions compile Roman law into a corpus that later Europe would rediscover.
body: The Digest, Code, and Institutes are legal monuments. Justinian’s wars and the later plague belong to the same ambitious, costly reign. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Humfress, in The Cambridge Companion to the Age of Justinian

title: Sui–Tang reunification of China
summary: The Sui reunite China; the Tang inherit and expand a restored imperial order.
body: Canals, exams, and a cosmopolitan capital at Chang’an followed. The Tang became a reference empire for East Asia. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Lewis, China’s Cosmopolitan Empire

title: Hijra and the first Muslim community
summary: Muhammad and his followers migrate from Mecca to Medina; the Islamic calendar begins here.
body: The umma became a political as well as religious community. Within a century, Arab-Muslim armies had overturned the Near Eastern balance of late antiquity. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Donner, Muhammad and the Believers; Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates

title: Battle of Tours / Poitiers
summary: Frankish forces under Charles Martel defeat an Umayyad raid in west-central Gaul.
body: Later European writers inflated the battle into a civilizational turning point. It was a significant check, not the sole reason Islamic rule did not take Gaul. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Fouracre, The Age of Charles Martel

title: Battle of Talas
summary: Abbasid and Tang forces clash in Central Asia; Chinese prisoners are later linked to paper-making in the Islamic world.
body: The military result halted Tang expansion westward. The paper story is traditional and partly legendary, but the cultural traffic was real. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Beckwith, Empires of the Silk Road

title: An Lushan rebellion
summary: A general’s revolt nearly destroys the Tang and kills a vast share of the registered population.
body: Census collapses are not simple death counts, but the social shock is not in doubt. Court power never fully recovered its early-Tang confidence. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan

title: Founding of Baghdad
summary: Al-Mansur founds Baghdad as the Abbasid capital, soon a world city of learning and trade.
body: The round city sat on Tigris commerce. Translation movements and later libraries made it a symbol of the Islamic golden age—again a later phrase, but the concentration of scholarship was real. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Kennedy, When Baghdad Ruled the Muslim World

title: Viking raid on Lindisfarne
summary: Seaborne attackers sack the monastery of Lindisfarne, a conventional start for the Viking Age in Britain.
body: Scandinavian expansion was already underway. The raid shocked literate churchmen and remains the textbook opening scene. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle; Barrett, in The Viking World

title: Heian period begins
summary: The court moves to Heian-kyō (Kyoto), opening a classical age of Japanese court culture.
body: The Tale of Genji and kana literature belong to this world. Political power later drifted to Fujiwara regents and then to warriors, but the cultural canon stayed. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Sansom, A History of Japan to 1334

title: Charlemagne crowned emperor
summary: Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne emperor in Rome on Christmas Day.
body: The act tied Frankish power to Roman and papal symbols. It did not recreate the old empire, but it created a western imperial idea that medieval Europe kept arguing about. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Einhard, Life of Charlemagne; McKitterick, Charlemagne

title: Song dynasty founded
summary: Zhao Kuangyin founds the Song, a state later famous for commerce, print, and a civil elite.
body: Northern then Southern Song faced powerful Inner Asian neighbours. Economic and intellectual vitality ran alongside military vulnerability. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Ebrey, The Cambridge Illustrated History of China

title: Baptism of Vladimir of Kyiv
summary: Vladimir of Kyiv accepts Byzantine Christianity, aligning Rus’ with Constantinople.
body: The Primary Chronicle’s story is stylized. The conversion still oriented East Slavic religion, law, and art toward the Orthodox world. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Franklin and Shepard, The Emergence of Rus 750–1200

title: Battle of Hastings
summary: William of Normandy defeats Harold and conquers England.
body: The Norman regime changed landholding, language at court, and England’s place in a cross-Channel world. The Bayeux Tapestry is propaganda and evidence together. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Bates, William the Conqueror

title: First Crusade
summary: Western expeditions take Jerusalem and plant Crusader states in the Levant.
body: Motives mixed piety, adventure, and politics. The massacre at Jerusalem and the new principalities recast Christian–Muslim relations in the eastern Mediterranean. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Riley-Smith, The First Crusade and the Idea of Crusading; Asbridge, The First Crusade

title: Temüjin proclaimed Chinggis Khan
summary: A kurultai names Temüjin Chinggis Khan, the starting gun of the Mongol Empire.
body: Within two generations Mongol armies had redrawn Eurasia. The empire was violent and also a structure for trade, relay posts, and unexpected cultural contact. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Ratchnevsky, Genghis Khan; Weatherford, Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World

title: Magna Carta
summary: English barons force King John to seal a charter of liberties at Runnymede.
body: Most clauses were feudal and local. Later lawyers turned the document into a symbol of due process and parliamentary constraint. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Holt, Magna Carta

title: Mongol sack of Baghdad
summary: Hülegü’s forces sack Baghdad and kill the last widely recognized Abbasid caliph there.
body: The destruction of libraries is proverbial and partly literary. The political fact is the end of a caliphal capital that had defined Sunni high culture for centuries. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Morgan, The Mongols; Kennedy, The Court of the Caliphs

title: Battle of ʿAyn Jālūt
summary: Mamluk forces defeat a Mongol army in Palestine, checking Mongol expansion into Egypt.
body: The victory did not end Mongol power in Persia, but it preserved the Mamluk sultanate and the last great medieval centre of Sunni military power in the west. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Amitai-Preiss, Mongols and Mamluks

title: Fall of Acre
summary: Mamluks take Acre, ending the Crusader kingdom on the Levantine coast.
body: Military orders relocated. The crusading idea lingered in Europe; the territorial project in Syria-Palestine did not. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Riley-Smith, The Crusades

title: Founding of Tenochtitlan
summary: Mexica settlers found Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco.
body: The city became the hub of the Aztec Triple Alliance. Spanish observers later struggled to describe its scale. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Smith, The Aztecs

title: Hundred Years’ War begins
summary: Edward III’s claim to France opens a long intermittent war between Plantagenet and Valois.
body: Crécy, Poitiers, Agincourt, and Joan of Arc are episodes in a longer state-building struggle. By 1453 England had lost almost all its continental possessions. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Sumption, The Hundred Years War

title: Black Death in Europe and the Near East
summary: Yersinia pestis kills a large fraction of the population from the western steppes to the Atlantic.
body: Mortality varied by place. Labour, piety, persecution of minorities, and the authority of Church and state all shifted in the aftermath. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Benedictow, The Black Death 1346–1353; Horrox, The Black Death

title: Ming dynasty founded
summary: Zhu Yuanzhang drives out Yuan rule and founds the Ming.
body: The new dynasty restored a Han-led empire, rebuilt institutions, and later sponsored the Zheng He voyages before turning more inward. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Mote and Twitchett, The Cambridge History of China, vol. 7

title: Joan of Arc at Orléans
summary: Joan of Arc helps lift the siege of Orléans and escorts Charles VII to Reims.
body: Captured and burned in 1431, she was later rehabilitated. The episode mixed popular prophecy, dynastic war, and the making of a French national saint. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Pernoud, Joan of Arc

title: Fall of Constantinople
summary: Mehmed II takes Constantinople and ends the Byzantine Empire.
body: Gunpowder siegecraft and a young sultan’s ambition closed a millennium of Roman rule in the east. The city became Ottoman imperial capital. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Runciman, The Fall of Constantinople 1453; Philippides and Hanak, The Siege and the Fall of Constantinople

title: Gutenberg Bible
summary: Johannes Gutenberg’s workshop prints a Latin Bible with movable metal type in Mainz.
body: Print did not appear from nowhere—China and Korea had earlier printing—but the European combination of type, press, paper, and market changed the scale of literate culture. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Febvre and Martin, The Coming of the Book

title: Fall of Granada
summary: The Catholic Monarchs take Granada, ending Muslim rule on the Iberian peninsula.
body: The same year saw the Alhambra Decree against Jews and Columbus’s first voyage. Iberian unification and Atlantic expansion were already entangled. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Harvey, Islamic Spain, 1250 to 1500

title: Columbus’s first voyage
summary: Columbus, sailing for Castile, reaches islands in the Caribbean and opens sustained contact between Europe and the Americas.
body: Norse landings had come and gone. 1492 began a demographic, ecological, and imperial exchange of planetary scale, catastrophic for many Indigenous societies. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Phillips and Phillips, The Worlds of Christopher Columbus; Crosby, The Columbian Exchange

title: Treaty of Tordesillas
summary: Spain and Portugal, with papal involvement, divide extra-European spheres along an Atlantic meridian.
body: Other powers ignored it. The treaty still structured Iberian claims in Brazil and the Indies and is a document of how Europe imagined the globe as partitionable. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Parry, The Spanish Seaborne Empire

title: Vasco da Gama reaches India
summary: A Portuguese fleet rounds Africa and arrives at Calicut, opening a sea route from Europe to the Indian Ocean.
body: The Indian Ocean already had a sophisticated trade world. Portuguese guns and cartaz licences forced a new, violent European presence into it. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Subrahmanyam, The Career and Legend of Vasco da Gama

title: Ninety-five Theses
summary: Martin Luther posts (or circulates) theses against indulgences, a spark of the Protestant Reformation.
body: Print, princely politics, and genuine pastoral anger combined. Western Christianity split, with consequences for states, literacy, and war. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Brecht, Martin Luther; MacCulloch, The Reformation

title: Magellan–Elcano circumnavigation
summary: A Spanish-backed expedition completes the first circumnavigation; Magellan dies in the Philippines.
body: The voyage proved the globe’s oceanic connectedness at terrible human cost. Elcano brought the Victoria home with a handful of survivors. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Pigafetta, Magellan’s Voyage; Bergreen, Over the Edge of the World

title: Fall of Tenochtitlan
summary: Cortés and a broad Indigenous alliance capture Tenochtitlan after siege and epidemic.
body: Spanish steel and horses mattered less than local politics and disease. The event is a hinge of the Columbian exchange and of colonial New Spain. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Restall, Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest; Díaz del Castillo, The True History of the Conquest of New Spain

title: Seizure of Atahualpa at Cajamarca
summary: Pizarro captures the Inca ruler Atahualpa, opening the rapid collapse of Tawantinsuyu’s political centre.
body: Civil war among the Inca, disease, and a tiny armed band combined. Silver from the Andes later fed a global monetary system. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Hemming, The Conquest of the Incas

title: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
summary: Copernicus publishes a heliocentric astronomy, dedicated to the pope, in the year of his death.
body: The book did not instantly dethrone Ptolemy. It started a long technical and theological argument that Galileo and Kepler would recast. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Gingerich, The Book Nobody Read; Copernicus, De revolutionibus

title: Battle of Lepanto
summary: A Holy League fleet defeats the Ottomans in the Gulf of Patras.
body: It was a famous Christian victory and not the end of Ottoman sea power. Cervantes fought there; painters never tired of it. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Capponi, Victory of the West

title: Spanish Armada
summary: Philip II’s invasion fleet fails against England, wrecked by fighting and weather.
body: The failure did not destroy Spain. It became a Protestant providential story and a marker of English naval self-image. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Martin and Parker, The Spanish Armada

title: Battle of Sekigahara
summary: Tokugawa Ieyasu wins a decisive battle that clears the way to the shogunate.
body: The Tokugawa order froze a warrior society into two centuries of relative peace, regulated foreign contact, and urban growth. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Totman, Early Modern Japan

title: Founding of Jamestown
summary: The Virginia Company plants a lasting English settlement on the James River.
body: Starving time, Powhatan relations, and tobacco shaped it. It is an origin point for English North America, not the first European or African presence. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Horn, A Land as God Made It

title: Sidereus Nuncius
summary: Galileo publishes telescopic discoveries: mountains on the Moon, new stars, and moons of Jupiter.
body: The little book made the sky empirical in a new way. Conflict with the Church came later and was about authority as much as astronomy. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Galilei, Sidereus Nuncius; Heilbron, Galileo

title: Thirty Years’ War
summary: A Bohemian revolt widens into a European war of religion, dynasty, and state-building.
body: Central Europe was devastated. The Peace of Westphalia (1648) became a later shorthand for a system of sovereign states—an over-neat lesson, but the settlement was real. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Wilson, The Thirty Years War

title: Qing conquest of Beijing
summary: Ming Beijing falls; the Manchu Qing become the new imperial dynasty.
body: Conquest of the whole empire took decades. The Qing built a multi-ethnic empire that lasted until 1912. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Wakeman, The Great Enterprise

title: Peace of Westphalia
summary: Treaties at Münster and Osnabrück end the Thirty Years’ War in the Empire and the Eighty Years’ War with Spain.
body: Cuius regio, territorial settlement, and a more plural Christian order in the Empire. Later theorists turned Westphalia into a myth of sovereignty. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Wilson, The Thirty Years War; Croxton, Westphalia

title: Execution of Charles I
summary: A parliamentary regime tries and beheads an English king after civil war.
body: The Commonwealth and then Cromwell’s Protectorate followed. The Restoration of 1660 did not erase the precedent of a king under law—and under the axe. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Worden, The English Civil Wars

title: Newton’s Principia
summary: Newton publishes the Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy, unifying celestial and terrestrial mechanics.
body: The book is technical and was read by few in full. Its prestige remade what “natural philosophy” could claim to be. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Newton, Principia; Cohen, The Newtonian Revolution

title: Glorious Revolution
summary: James II is displaced; William and Mary take the throne under a new constitutional settlement.
body: It was glorious mainly for its later Whig narrators, and it was also an invasion. The Bill of Rights and parliamentary supremacy became the durable result. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Pincus, 1688

title: Battle of Plassey
summary: Clive’s East India Company force, with Indian allies, defeats Siraj-ud-Daulah and opens Bengal to Company rule.
body: Bribery and defection decided the day as much as muskets. Plassey is a hinge from trading company to territorial colonial power. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Marshall, Bengal: The British Bridgehead

title: Seven Years’ War
summary: A global war among European powers redraws North America, the Caribbean, and India.
body: Some historians call it a first world war. Britain emerged with a larger empire and a larger debt—both causes of later revolutions. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Anderson, Crucible of War; Szabo, The Seven Years War in Europe

title: Watt’s separate condenser patent
summary: James Watt patents a more efficient steam engine, a key piece of industrial power technology.
body: Newcomen came first; railways came later. Watt’s partnership with Boulton still marks a shift from pumping mines to driving mills. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Hills, Power from Steam

title: Cook on the east coast of Australia
summary: James Cook charts the east coast of Australia and claims it for Britain, ignoring existing Aboriginal sovereignty.
body: Polynesian and Aboriginal histories run far deeper. Cook’s voyage still became the legal myth of British Australia. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Beaglehole, The Life of Captain James Cook

title: Declaration of Independence
summary: Thirteen colonies declare independence from Britain in a document that became a global political text.
body: The war was already underway. The Declaration’s equality language sat beside slavery; that contradiction shaped later American history. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Maier, American Scripture

title: The Wealth of Nations
summary: Adam Smith publishes an inquiry into the nature and causes of the wealth of nations.
body: Smith was a moral philosopher, not a prophet of unregulated capital. The book still became a founding text of political economy. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations

title: Siege of Yorktown
summary: Franco-American forces trap Cornwallis at Yorktown, effectively winning the War of Independence.
body: French sea power was decisive. The 1783 peace recognized a new republic and left Loyalists, Indigenous nations, and enslaved people in unresolved positions. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Middlekauff, The Glorious Cause

title: French Revolution begins
summary: The Bastille falls and a revolutionary crisis in France becomes a European turning point.
body: Fiscal collapse, Enlightenment argument, and popular action combined. The decade that followed exported both rights talk and mass war. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Doyle, The Oxford History of the French Revolution

title: Haitian Revolution begins
summary: Enslaved people in Saint-Domingue rise, beginning the only successful slave revolution to found a lasting state.
body: Toussaint Louverture and later Dessalines fought French, Spanish, and British forces. Independence in 1804 terrified slaveholding powers. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: James, The Black Jacobins; Dubois, Avengers of the New World

title: Execution of Louis XVI
summary: The French Republic guillotines the former king, internationalizing the revolution.
body: War and the Terror were already in motion. The execution made compromise with old-regime Europe far harder. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Doyle, The Oxford History of the French Revolution

title: Jenner’s smallpox vaccination
summary: Edward Jenner demonstrates cowpox inoculation as protection against smallpox.
body: Variolation already existed. Jenner’s method was safer and became the root of modern vaccination, later ending smallpox as a human disease. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Baxby, Jenner’s Smallpox Vaccine

title: Battle of the Nile
summary: Nelson destroys the French fleet at Aboukir Bay, stranding Bonaparte’s Egyptian expedition.
body: The campaign still brought European scholars to Egypt. Militarily, Britain had reasserted control of the Mediterranean approaches. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Rodger, The Command of the Ocean

title: 18 Brumaire
summary: Bonaparte’s coup ends the Directory and opens the Consulate.
body: The revolution’s political experiments gave way to a military-authoritarian settlement that still claimed to save 1789 from itself. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Lefebvre, Napoleon

title: Haitian independence
summary: Dessalines proclaims the independence of Haiti, the second independent state in the Americas.
body: Diplomatic isolation and a later French indemnity burdened the new country. The political fact of Black sovereignty remained explosive. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Dubois, Haiti: The Aftershocks of History

title: Napoleon crowned emperor
summary: Napoleon crowns himself emperor in Notre-Dame, converting the revolutionary republic into a hereditary empire.
body: David’s painting fixed the image. The Civil Code and administrative state were the more lasting Napoleonic exports. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Tulard, Napoleon; Woloch, Napoleon and His Collaborators

title: Battle of Austerlitz
summary: Napoleon defeats a Russo-Austrian army in his most famous set-piece victory.
body: The Holy Roman Empire was wound up the next year. Austerlitz seemed to make French hegemony in Europe look permanent. It was not. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Chandler, The Campaigns of Napoleon

title: British abolition of the slave trade
summary: Parliament bans the British Atlantic slave trade, then tries to police others at sea.
body: Enslavement in British colonies continued until the 1830s. Abolition was a moral campaign and an imperial policy instrument at once. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Anstey, The Atlantic Slave Trade and British Abolition

title: Grito de Dolores
summary: Miguel Hidalgo’s call to arms opens the mass phase of Mexican independence.
body: The insurgency was social as well as anti-colonial. Independence was completed in 1821 on quite different political terms. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Hamnett, A Concise History of Mexico

title: War of 1812
summary: The United States and Britain fight a messy war over impressment, trade, and the North American interior.
body: Indigenous nations were the biggest losers. Americans remembered New Orleans; Canadians remembered the burning of York and a surviving colonies story. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Taylor, The Civil War of 1812

title: Battle of Leipzig
summary: A coalition smashes Napoleon’s army in the Battle of the Nations.
body: It was the largest Napoleonic land battle. France was forced back toward its “natural” frontiers, and the endgame of 1814–15 began. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Lieven, Russia Against Napoleon

title: Congress of Vienna
summary: Allied diplomats rebuild a conservative European order after Napoleon.
body: Legitimacy and balance of power were the watchwords. The settlement kept a general European peace among the great powers for decades, at the price of repressed national and liberal movements. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Schroeder, The Transformation of European Politics; Zamoyski, Rites of Peace

title: Battle of Waterloo
summary: Wellington and Blücher defeat Napoleon, ending the Hundred Days.
body: The battle closed a quarter-century of French revolutionary and imperial war. Saint Helena followed; so did a long British self-image as the army that stopped him. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Hofschröer, 1815: The Waterloo Campaign; Adkin, The Waterloo Companion

title: Battle of Boyacá
summary: Bolívar’s victory at Boyacá secures the independence of New Granada.
body: Spanish American independence was a mosaic of wars, not a single campaign. Bolívar’s later disappointment with unity is part of the same story. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Lynch, Simón Bolívar

title: First Opium War
summary: Britain forces Qing China open after a conflict rooted in opium, trade, and sovereignty.
body: The Treaty of Nanjing ceded Hong Kong and imposed unequal terms. It begins what Chinese historiography calls the century of humiliation. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Fay, The Opium War; Lovell, The Opium War

title: Treaty of Waitangi
summary: The British Crown and many Māori chiefs sign a treaty whose two language versions still disagree.
body: It is New Zealand’s founding constitutional puzzle. Land, sovereignty, and the Waitangi Tribunal are live politics, not closed history. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Orange, The Treaty of Waitangi

title: Taiping Rebellion
summary: Hong Xiuquan’s millenarian movement fights the Qing in one of the deadliest wars in history.
body: Deaths ran into the tens of millions. The Qing survived with foreign and regional help, but the dynasty was mortally weakened. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Spence, God’s Chinese Son; Platt, Autumn in the Heavenly Kingdom

title: Indian Rebellion of 1857
summary: Sepoy mutiny and civilian uprising shake Company rule; the Crown takes over India.
body: British reprisals were savage. Nationalist memory later called it the First War of Independence; it was also a patchwork of local grievances. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Bayly, Indian Society and the Making of the British Empire; Dalrymple, The Last Mughal

title: On the Origin of Species
summary: Darwin publishes a theory of evolution by natural selection that remade biology and cultural debate.
body: Wallace arrived at a similar mechanism. The book’s slow, documentary style hid a philosophical explosion. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Darwin, On the Origin of Species; Browne, Charles Darwin: The Power of Place

title: American Civil War
summary: Eleven slaveholding states secede; the Union fights to restore the United States and, increasingly, to destroy slavery.
body: Industrial war, emancipation, and a stronger federal state followed. Reconstruction’s unfinished work is part of the war’s meaning. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: McPherson, Battle Cry of Freedom

title: Emancipation Proclamation
summary: Lincoln declares enslaved people in rebel-held territory free, tying the Union war to abolition.
body: It was a war measure, not a statute ending slavery everywhere. The 13th Amendment completed the legal break. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Foner, The Fiery Trial

title: Meiji Restoration
summary: Tokugawa rule ends; a new Meiji state begins a crash programme of reform and industrialization.
body: Charter Oath, conscription, and imported institutions remade Japan. Within a generation it was a great power—and an empire. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Jansen, The Making of Modern Japan

title: Suez Canal opened
summary: The canal joins the Mediterranean to the Red Sea and shortens Europe–Asia sea routes.
body: French engineering and Egyptian labour built it; Britain later bought control. The canal became a strategic obsession of later empires. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Karabell, Parting the Desert

title: German Empire proclaimed
summary: William I is proclaimed German emperor at Versailles after the Franco-Prussian War.
body: Bismarck’s unification created a new great power in the middle of Europe. The French indemnity and lost provinces stored up a future war. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Clark, Iron Kingdom; Wawro, The Franco-Prussian War

title: Berlin Conference
summary: European powers set rules for claiming Africa, accelerating the Scramble.
body: Africans were not at the table. The conference did not invent partition, but it regularized a land grab with catastrophic local consequences. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Pakenham, The Scramble for Africa; Wesseling, Divide and Rule

title: First Sino-Japanese War
summary: Meiji Japan defeats Qing China and takes Taiwan, shocking the regional order.
body: Korea became the prize. The war announced Japan as an imperial power and deepened China’s late-Qing crisis. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Paine, The Sino-Japanese War of 1894–1895

title: Discovery of X-rays
summary: Wilhelm Röntgen detects X-rays, opening a new medical and physical technique.
body: The public sensation was immediate. Radiology, crystallography, and a new physics of radiation followed. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Glasser, Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen

title: Spanish–American War
summary: The United States defeats Spain and takes overseas colonies, including the Philippines and Puerto Rico.
body: Cuba was the public cause; empire was the result. The Philippine–American War that followed was longer and bloodier than the war with Spain. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Pérez, The War of 1898; Silbey, A War of Frontier and Empire

title: Boxer Uprising
summary: The Boxer movement and a Qing declaration of war bring an eight-nation invasion of north China.
body: The occupation of Beijing and a huge indemnity further reduced Qing sovereignty. Nationalist memory treated the Boxers as both patriots and a warning. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Esherick, The Origins of the Boxer Uprising

title: Wright Flyer
summary: The Wright brothers make the first sustained, controlled powered flights at Kitty Hawk.
body: Others were close. Within a decade the aeroplane was a weapon as well as a wonder. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Crouch, The Bishop’s Boys

title: Russo-Japanese War
summary: Japan defeats Russia, the first modern victory of an Asian power over a European empire.
body: Mukden and Tsushima stunned observers. The war fed Russian revolution in 1905 and Japanese imperial confidence in Korea and Manchuria. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Jukes, The Russo-Japanese War

title: Einstein’s annus mirabilis
summary: Einstein publishes papers on the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion, and special relativity.
body: A patent clerk remade physics. The photoelectric paper later underpinned the quantum, and E = mc² entered the century’s political history via the bomb. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Isaacson, Einstein; Pais, Subtle is the Lord

title: Fall of the Qing
summary: The 1911 Revolution ends China’s last imperial dynasty and proclaims a republic.
body: Yuan Shikai, warlords, and later the Nationalists and Communists inherited the wreckage. Dynastic time, as a political form, was over. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Spence, The Search for Modern China

title: Assassination of Franz Ferdinand
summary: Gavrilo Princip kills the Austro-Hungarian heir in Sarajevo, triggering the July Crisis.
body: The murder did not make a world war inevitable; alliance politics, timetables, and miscalculation did. It remains the spark. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Clark, The Sleepwalkers; McMeekin, July 1914

title: The Great War begins
summary: General European war opens after the July Crisis and becomes a global conflict.
body: Industrial killing, blockade, and mass conscription defined it. Four empires would not survive the peace. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Strachan, The First World War; Keegan, The First World War

title: Gallipoli campaign
summary: Allied landings on the Gallipoli peninsula fail to open the Straits.
body: ANZAC memory, Turkish national memory, and a British strategic fiasco occupy the same beaches. The Ottomans held. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Prior, Gallipoli

title: Armenian Genocide
summary: Ottoman authorities deport and kill huge numbers of Armenians during the war.
body: Scholarship treats the destruction as genocide; official Turkish denial remains a political fact. The event is central to modern human-rights memory. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Suny, “They Can Live in the Desert but Nowhere Else”; Akçam, The Young Turks’ Crime Against Humanity

title: Battle of Verdun
summary: Germany and France grind each other down in a ten-month battle around Verdun.
body: Falkenhayn’s attritional idea met a French decision that the place could not be yielded. The ossuary at Douaumont is the commentary. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Horne, The Price of Glory

title: Battle of the Somme
summary: The Anglo-French Somme offensive opens with catastrophic British losses on the first day.
body: The battle lasted into November. Tanks appeared; so did a lasting British memory of futility, which historians have since complicated. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Philpott, Bloody Victory

title: Russian Revolution of 1917
summary: The Romanov monarchy collapses; Bolsheviks take power in October and exit the world war.
body: Two revolutions, then civil war. The Soviet experiment became the other pole of the 20th century’s political map. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Figes, A People’s Tragedy; Fitzpatrick, The Russian Revolution

title: United States enters World War I
summary: The United States declares war on Germany, tipping the resource balance of the conflict.
body: Unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram were the public triggers. American troops and credit mattered in 1918. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Kennedy, Over Here

title: Armistice of 11 November 1918
summary: Fighting on the Western Front stops at the eleventh hour; the German, Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman, and Russian empires are already broken or breaking.
body: The peace treaties that followed stored up grievances. The influenza pandemic was killing more people than the armies by then. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: MacMillan, Peacemakers; Stevenson, With Our Backs to the Wall

title: Influenza pandemic of 1918–19
summary: A novel influenza kills tens of millions worldwide in the war’s last year and after.
body: Wartime censorship hid the early spread. The death toll likely exceeded that of the fighting, with a grim preference for young adults. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Crosby, America’s Forgotten Pandemic; Spinney, Pale Rider

title: Treaty of Versailles
summary: The treaty with Germany imposes territorial loss, disarmament, and reparations, and founds the League of Nations.
body: Keynes called it a Carthaginian peace; others thought it too mild. It was a political fact Germans could be taught to hate. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: MacMillan, Peacemakers; Keynes, The Economic Consequences of the Peace

title: Jallianwala Bagh massacre
summary: British troops fire on an unarmed crowd at Amritsar, a turning point in Indian nationalism.
body: Dyer’s justification shocked even parts of the British establishment. Gandhi’s mass politics gained a moral wound to organize around. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Collett, The Butcher of Amritsar

title: Irish Free State
summary: The Anglo-Irish Treaty settlement produces the Irish Free State and a partitioned island.
body: Civil war followed in the south. Northern Ireland remained in the United Kingdom, a conflict postponed rather than solved. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Foster, Modern Ireland 1600–1972

title: Fleming observes penicillin
summary: Alexander Fleming notices the antibacterial effect of Penicillium, the start of the antibiotic era.
body: Florey, Chain, and wartime production made it a medicine. Infectious disease, surgery, and life expectancy changed. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Lax, The Mold in Dr. Florey’s Coat

title: Wall Street Crash
summary: US stock prices collapse, marking the visible onset of the Great Depression.
body: Banking failures, unemployment, and beggar-thy-neighbour trade followed. Politics in Germany, the US, and the empires all shifted. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Kindleberger, The World in Depression; Galbraith, The Great Crash 1929

title: Japanese invasion of Manchuria
summary: The Kwantung Army seizes Manchuria after the Mukden Incident, defying Tokyo’s caution and the League.
body: Manchukuo was a puppet state. The League’s failure to reverse the grab advertised the weakness of the interwar order. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Young, Japan’s Total Empire

title: Hitler appointed chancellor
summary: Hindenburg appoints Hitler chancellor; the Nazi seizure of power follows within months.
body: It was a legal appointment in a dying republic, then a dictatorship. The Reichstag fire, Enabling Act, and Gleichschaltung closed the gap. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Kershaw, Hitler: 1889–1936 Hubris; Evans, The Coming of the Third Reich

title: Long March
summary: Chinese Communists retreat from Jiangxi to Yan’an, a myth of survival that made Mao the party’s centre.
body: Losses were enormous. The later cult of the March was propaganda; the political result—Mao’s ascendancy—was real. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Salisbury, The Long March; Sun Shuyun, The Long March

title: Spanish Civil War
summary: A military rising against the Republic becomes a European proxy war and a fascist victory under Franco.
body: Guernica, the International Brigades, and non-intervention are the remembered emblems. Spain then sat out 1939–45 in dictatorship. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Beevor, The Battle for Spain; Preston, The Spanish Civil War

title: Nanjing Massacre
summary: After taking Nanjing, Japanese forces kill and rape on a mass scale.
body: Death tolls are still argued; the atrocity is not. It remains a live wound in East Asian politics. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Chang, The Rape of Nanking; Fogel, The Nanjing Massacre in History and Historiography

title: Anschluss and Munich
summary: Nazi Germany annexes Austria and, at Munich, is handed the Sudetenland.
body: Appeasement had reasons as well as a later bad name. March 1939’s occupation of Prague ended the illusion that Hitler wanted only Germans. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Kershaw, Hitler: 1936–1945 Nemesis; Faber, Munich, 1938

title: Invasion of Poland
summary: Germany invades Poland; Britain and France declare war. The Soviet Union invades from the east on 17 September.
body: The Molotov–Ribbentrop pact had already partitioned Eastern Europe on paper. Blitzkrieg in Poland was the public opening of a second world war. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Overy, 1939; Kochanski, The Eagle Unbowed

title: Fall of France
summary: Germany defeats France in six weeks; a collaborationist regime sits at Vichy.
body: Dunkirk saved a British army. The shock of 1940 convinced much of the world that Nazi Germany might win. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Jackson, The Fall of France

title: Battle of Britain
summary: The RAF denies the Luftwaffe air superiority over Britain, ending the immediate threat of invasion.
body: Radar, production, and German strategic oscillation all mattered. Churchill’s sentences did too, as politics. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Overy, The Battle of Britain

title: Operation Barbarossa
summary: Nazi Germany invades the Soviet Union in a war of annihilation.
body: The eastern front became the decisive and most murderous theatre. Siege, starvation, and the Holocaust intensified in its shadow. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Stahel, Operation Barbarossa and Germany’s Defeat in the East; Snyder, Bloodlands

title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
summary: Japan attacks the US Pacific Fleet, bringing the United States fully into the world war.
body: Hitler’s declaration of war on the United States days later fused the European and Pacific wars into one coalition conflict. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Prange, At Dawn We Slept; Dower, War Without Mercy

title: Wannsee Conference
summary: Nazi officials coordinate the already-begun mass murder of Europe’s Jews as a continent-wide “Final Solution.”
body: Killing was underway in 1941. Wannsee is a bureaucratic landmark of genocide, not its origin. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Roseman, The Villa, the Lake, the Meeting; Longerich, Holocaust

title: Battle of Stalingrad
summary: The Red Army encircles the German 6th Army; the strategic initiative in Europe passes to the Allies.
body: The human cost on both sides was extreme. After Stalingrad, German victory in the east was no longer a serious prospect. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Beevor, Stalingrad; Glantz and House, To the Gates of Stalingrad

title: Normandy landings
summary: Allied forces land in Normandy and open a lasting western front against Germany.
body: Soviet offensives in the east were already shattering the Wehrmacht. D-Day still decided that western Europe would be liberated from the west. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Beevor, D-Day; Hastings, Overlord

title: Yalta Conference
summary: Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin bargain over the end of the European war and the shape of the peace.
body: Poland, occupation zones, and the United Nations were on the table. Later American politics treated Yalta as a betrayal; it was also a recognition of where the Red Army already stood. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Plokhy, Yalta

title: German surrender
summary: Nazi Germany surrenders unconditionally; the war in Europe ends.
body: Hitler was already dead. Occupation, denazification, and the division of Germany filled the space the Reich had occupied. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Kershaw, The End; Bessel, Germany 1945

title: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
summary: The United States detonates atomic bombs over two Japanese cities; the Soviet Union enters the Pacific war; Japan surrenders.
body: Debate over necessity and morality is permanent. The bombings opened the nuclear age as a political fact, not a thought experiment. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Rhodes, The Making of the Atomic Bomb; Hasegawa, Racing the Enemy

title: United Nations Charter
summary: Fifty governments sign the UN Charter in San Francisco, replacing the League with a new collective-security body.
body: The Security Council froze great-power inequality into the system. The Charter remains the basic law of inter-state ritual, if not of behaviour. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Schlesinger, Act of Creation

title: Independence and Partition of India
summary: British India is partitioned into India and Pakistan amid mass violence and refugee flight.
body: Independence ended the Raj. Partition killed and displaced millions and set up wars over Kashmir that have not closed. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Khan, The Great Partition; Talbot and Singh, The Partition of India

title: State of Israel proclaimed
summary: Israel declares independence as the British Mandate ends; war with neighbouring states and the Palestinian Nakba follow.
body: UN partition, Zionist state-building, and Palestinian dispossession are one event with two enduring national narratives. The conflict remains open. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Morris, 1948; Khalidi, The Iron Cage

title: People’s Republic of China founded
summary: Mao Zedong proclaims the PRC after the Communist victory in the civil war.
body: The Nationalists retreated to Taiwan. A quarter of humanity entered a revolutionary state that would remake land, family, and later the world economy. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Spence, The Search for Modern China; Westad, Decisive Encounters

title: Korean War
summary: North Korea invades the South; US-led UN forces and then China fight a war that freezes the peninsula’s division.
body: The armistice still holds, without a peace treaty. Korea became the template of limited but savage Cold War conflict. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Cumings, The Korean War; Hastings, The Korean War

title: Structure of DNA
summary: Watson and Crick, using Franklin’s and Wilkins’s data, propose the double helix.
body: The paper is short; the credit dispute is long. Molecular biology as an industry and as a picture of life starts here. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Judson, The Eighth Day of Creation; Maddox, Rosalind Franklin

title: Brown v. Board of Education
summary: The US Supreme Court rules segregated public schools unconstitutional.
body: Implementation took years of conflict. The decision is a landmark of the civil rights movement and of constitutional law. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Kluger, Simple Justice

title: Bandung Conference
summary: Asian and African states meet in Indonesia to assert a voice outside the two Cold War blocs.
body: Non-alignment was never simple neutrality. Bandung is a marker of decolonization as a political project, not only a series of flags. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Wright, The Color Curtain; Lee, Making a World after Empire

title: Suez Crisis
summary: Egypt nationalizes the canal; Britain, France, and Israel invade, then retreat under US and Soviet pressure.
body: Nasser emerged stronger. The episode advertised that the old European empires could no longer act alone in the Middle East. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Kyle, Suez; Louis and Owen, Suez 1956

title: Sputnik 1
summary: The Soviet Union orbits the first artificial satellite, opening the space age and a US panic about science.
body: The launcher was a missile. Education, prestige, and nuclear delivery were all in play. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Dickson, Sputnik; McDougall, The Heavens and the Earth

title: Cuban Revolution
summary: Batista flees; Castro’s movement takes Havana and soon aligns with the Soviet Union.
body: Land reform, nationalization, and a US embargo followed. Cuba became the Cold War’s Caribbean flashpoint. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Pérez-Stable, The Cuban Revolution

title: Berlin Wall
summary: East Germany seals the Berlin border with a wall, stopping the refugee drain to the West.
body: The wall became the concrete image of the Cold War. It fell in 1989 faster than most experts expected. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Taylor, The Berlin Wall; Harrison, Driving the Soviets up the Wall

title: Cuban Missile Crisis
summary: Soviet missiles in Cuba bring the United States and USSR to the edge of nuclear war.
body: A naval “quarantine,” secret Turkey-missile bargaining, and luck all featured. Crisis management became a Cold War skill and a myth. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Allison and Zelikow, Essence of Decision; Fursenko and Naftali, One Hell of a Gamble

title: Civil Rights Act of 1964
summary: US federal law bans segregation in public accommodations and discrimination in employment.
body: It followed Birmingham, the March on Washington, and Kennedy’s assassination. Voting rights legislation the next year attacked the other half of Jim Crow. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Branch, Pillar of Fire

title: Six-Day War
summary: Israel defeats Egypt, Jordan, and Syria and occupies the West Bank, Gaza, Sinai, and the Golan Heights.
body: The map of the conflict has been the 1967 map ever since. Occupation, settlements, and UN 242 begin here as a political structure. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Oren, Six Days of War; Louis and Shlaim, The 1967 Arab-Israeli War

title: Prague Spring crushed
summary: Warsaw Pact troops occupy Czechoslovakia and end a reform Communist experiment.
body: “Socialism with a human face” became a warning. 1968 elsewhere was students and Vietnam; in Prague it was tanks. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Williams, The Prague Spring and its Aftermath

title: Apollo 11
summary: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walk on the Moon; a global television audience watches.
body: It was a Cold War victory and a genuine exploration. The scientific harvest continued; human deep-space travel did not, for decades. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Chaikin, A Man on the Moon

title: 1973 oil crisis
summary: Arab producers embargo oil during the October War; prices quadruple and the postwar growth model stutters.
body: Stagflation, energy politics, and a richer Gulf followed. Industrial societies discovered a vulnerability they have not forgotten. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Yergin, The Prize

title: Fall of Saigon
summary: North Vietnamese forces take Saigon, ending the Vietnam War and unifying the country under Hanoi.
body: American defeat reshaped US politics and military doctrine. For Vietnam it was independence, reconstruction, and later a different kind of opening. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Karnow, Vietnam; Hastings, Vietnam: An Epic Tragedy

title: Iranian Revolution
summary: The Shah falls; an Islamic Republic under Khomeini replaces a US-backed monarchy.
body: The hostage crisis and the Iran–Iraq War followed. Political Islam as a revolutionary state form had a capital. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Keddie, Modern Iran; Abrahamian, Iran Between Two Revolutions

title: Soviet invasion of Afghanistan
summary: The USSR occupies Afghanistan to prop up a Communist government; a long insurgency follows.
body: US, Pakistani, and Saudi backing of the mujahideen had afterlives no sponsor fully controlled. The war bled the late Soviet state. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Kalínovsky, A Long Goodbye; Coll, Ghost Wars

title: Smallpox eradicated
summary: WHO declares smallpox eradicated, the first human disease wiped out by a public-health campaign.
body: Jenner’s method, later freeze-dried vaccine, and a surveillance-containment strategy closed a killer that had shaped civilizations. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Fenner et al., Smallpox and its Eradication

title: Solidarity in Poland
summary: A Gdańsk shipyard strike becomes a mass independent union, the first of its kind in the Soviet bloc.
body: Martial law repressed it; it returned. John Paul II, economic failure, and working-class organization all featured. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Ash, The Polish Revolution

title: Chernobyl disaster
summary: A reactor explosion in Ukraine spreads radioactive contamination across Europe and credibility damage across the USSR.
body: Gorbachev later said it was a turning point of glasnost. Energy, secrecy, and environmental fear all changed register. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Plokhy, Chernobyl; Higginbotham, Midnight in Chernobyl

title: Tiananmen Square crackdown
summary: The Chinese Communist Party crushes a Beijing protest movement with the army.
body: Deaths remain officially uncounted. Economic reform continued; political opening did not. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Brook, Quelling the People; Nathan and Link, The Tiananmen Papers

title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
summary: A bungled East German press conference opens the wall; crowds finish the job.
body: 1989 in Eastern Europe was a season, not a night. The wall’s end remains the emblem of the Cold War’s civilian collapse. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Sarotte, 1989; Sebestyen, Revolution 1989

title: Dissolution of the Soviet Union
summary: The USSR is voted out of existence; fifteen republics become internationally recognized states.
body: The August coup failed; the economy was already breaking. Nuclear inheritance, oligarchic privatization, and later revanchism all start in this wreckage. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Plokhy, The Last Empire; Kotkin, Armageddon Averted

title: South African election of 1994
summary: South Africa holds its first universal elections; Nelson Mandela becomes president and apartheid as law ends.
body: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission followed. Economic inequality did not vanish with the pass laws. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Sparks, Tomorrow Is Another Country; Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom

title: Rwandan genocide
summary: Hutu Power militias and many civilians murder Tutsi and moderate Hutu on a mass scale in about a hundred days.
body: The UN and major powers failed to stop it. The later Congo wars grew in part from the same explosion. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Des Forges, Leave None to Tell the Story; Gourevitch, We Wish to Inform You…

title: Hong Kong handover
summary: Britain returns Hong Kong to China under a “one country, two systems” formula.
body: The later national security law is part of the same unfinished argument about autonomy. 1997 was an imperial sunset and a Chinese national milestone. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Tsang, A Modern History of Hong Kong

title: September 11 attacks
summary: Al-Qaeda hijackers destroy the Twin Towers and strike the Pentagon, killing nearly 3,000 people.
body: The US-led wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, and a vast security apparatus, followed. Domestic politics in many countries shifted around the event. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: The 9/11 Commission Report; Wright, The Looming Tower

title: Iraq War
summary: A US-led coalition invades Iraq and topples Saddam Hussein on disputed claims about weapons of mass destruction.
body: Occupation, insurgency, and later ISIS grew from the wreckage of the Baʿthist state. The war’s justifications did not survive inspection. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Gordon and Trainor, Cobra II; Packer, The Assassins’ Gate

title: Global financial crisis
summary: A US housing and banking crash becomes a global credit crisis and a deep recession.
body: Lehman’s failure is the emblem. Austerity, populism, and a long argument about inequality followed in the next decade. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Tooze, Crashed; Bernanke, The Federal Reserve and the Financial Crisis

title: Arab Spring
summary: Uprisings unseat rulers in Tunisia, Egypt, Libya, and Yemen and shake Syria into a long war.
body: Outcomes diverged from democratic transition to civil war and restoration. The term is a journalist’s umbrella over many local histories. Editorial draft for this timeline, not a substitute for specialist literature.
sources: Ghonim, Revolution 2.0; Lynch, The Arab Uprising

title: Paris climate agreement
summary: Nearly every state agrees to limit global warming, with nationally determined contributions rather than a single binding cap.
